title: Price determination
overview: This topic brings demand and supply together to explain how a market settles on an equilibrium price and quantity, and how market forces remove excess demand and excess supply. It is the analytical engine behind almost every Theme 1 and Theme 3 answer: if you can shift the right curve, in the right direction, and explain the adjustment process step by step, you can analyse any real-world market change the exam throws at you.
objectives: Define equilibrium, excess demand and excess supply and identify them on a diagram
Explain step by step how market forces eliminate a disequilibrium
Analyse the effect of shifts in demand and/or supply on equilibrium price and quantity, including simultaneous shifts
Calculate equilibrium price and quantity from linear demand and supply equations
Use elasticity to explain why the same shift has different effects in different markets
Apply the model to real UK and global markets and evaluate its assumptions

sections.heading: Equilibrium: where plans match
sections.body:
A market is any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers together. Buyers' plans are summarised by the **demand curve** (quantity demanded at each price, ceteris paribus) and sellers' plans by the **supply curve** (quantity supplied at each price). Each curve on its own says nothing about what price will actually be charged. Price is determined only when the two are combined.

**Equilibrium** is the price at which the quantity consumers wish to buy exactly equals the quantity producers wish to sell. At that price the market clears: there is no unsold stock piling up and no frustrated buyers who would pay the going price but cannot find the good. Because plans are consistent, there is no internal pressure for price to change. That is what equilibrium means in economics: a position of rest, not necessarily a position that is good or fair.

Two points are worth stating precisely in the exam:

- Equilibrium is found where the curves **intersect**, giving the equilibrium price (Pe) and quantity (Qe). Always label both on the axes with dashed guide lines.
- Equilibrium persists **only until a condition of demand or supply changes**. A change in income, tastes, costs or technology shifts a curve, creates a disequilibrium at the old price, and the market moves to a new equilibrium.

sections.heading: Excess demand, excess supply and how market forces remove them
sections.body:
**Excess supply** (a surplus) exists when, at the current price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. **Excess demand** (a shortage) exists when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. On the diagram, draw a horizontal line at the disequilibrium price and read off both quantities: the horizontal gap between the curves is the size of the surplus or shortage.

The adjustment process is a chain of reasoning examiners reward, so write it out in full:

- **Excess supply (price above Pe):** unsold stock accumulates, so firms cut prices to clear it. As price falls, quantity demanded **extends** (a movement along D) and quantity supplied **contracts** (a movement along S) because production becomes less profitable. The surplus shrinks until it disappears at Pe.
- **Excess demand (price below Pe):** queues and empty shelves appear, so consumers bid up prices and firms see they can raise prices without losing sales. As price rises, quantity demanded contracts and quantity supplied extends, until the shortage disappears at Pe.

Notice the vocabulary: a change in the good's **own price** causes **movements along** the curves (extensions and contractions), never shifts. Mixing these up is the single most common way students lose analysis marks in this topic.

The model assumes prices are **flexible** and that buyers and sellers respond quickly. In some markets (wholesale energy, shares, foreign exchange) prices adjust within seconds. In others (rented housing, labour, concert tickets sold at a fixed face value) prices are sticky, so shortages or surpluses can persist for a long time. That contrast is a strong source of evaluation.

sections.heading: Shifts in demand and supply: the four basic cases
sections.body:
Any real-world event should be analysed in three steps: (1) decide whether it affects **demand** or **supply** (or both) and why, using a named determinant; (2) decide the **direction** of the shift; (3) trace the adjustment from the old to the new equilibrium, explaining the disequilibrium that appears at the old price.

- **Increase in demand** (e.g. higher incomes for a normal good, a successful advertising campaign): D shifts right. At the old price there is excess demand, price is bid up, supply extends. **Price and quantity both rise.**
- **Decrease in demand** (e.g. a cheaper substitute appears): D shifts left. Excess supply at the old price; price falls and supply contracts. **Price and quantity both fall.**
- **Increase in supply** (e.g. lower raw material costs, better technology, a subsidy): S shifts right. Excess supply at the old price; price falls and demand extends. **Price falls, quantity rises.**
- **Decrease in supply** (e.g. poor harvest, higher energy costs, an indirect tax): S shifts left. Excess demand at the old price; price rises and demand contracts. **Price rises, quantity falls.**

A useful check: demand shifts move price and quantity in the **same** direction; supply shifts move them in **opposite** directions. This is exactly how economists infer from data which side of a market changed. If house prices and transactions both rose, demand is the likely driver; if petrol prices rose while litres sold fell, supply is the more likely cause.

sections.heading: Simultaneous shifts and the role of elasticity
sections.body:
Real markets rarely experience one shock at a time. When both curves shift, one variable can be predicted and the other is **indeterminate** without knowing the relative size of the shifts.

- D increases and S increases: quantity definitely rises; price rises if the demand shift is larger, falls if the supply shift is larger, and is unchanged if they are equal (see the diagram).
- D increases and S decreases: price definitely rises; quantity is indeterminate.
- D decreases and S increases: price definitely falls; quantity is indeterminate.
- D decreases and S decreases: quantity definitely falls; price is indeterminate.

**Elasticity decides the split between price and quantity.** For a given shift in demand, the more price inelastic supply is, the more the adjustment comes through price rather than quantity. UK housing is the classic case: supply is very inelastic in the short run because planning and construction take years, so rising demand shows up mainly as higher prices and rents. Similarly, for a given shift in supply, the more price inelastic demand is, the larger the price change. That is why a modest disruption to oil or gas supply produces a dramatic price spike: consumers cannot quickly cut their use of heating or fuel.

Time matters too. Supply becomes more elastic in the long run as firms build capacity and new firms enter, so a demand increase that first causes a sharp price rise may later be followed by a supply increase that brings price partly back down. Top answers distinguish short-run and long-run equilibria explicitly.

sections.heading: Calculating equilibrium
sections.body:
You may be given linear equations. Set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied and solve.

Suppose Qd = 120 − 4P and Qs = 6P − 30 (P in £, Q in thousands per week). Then 120 − 4P = 6P − 30, so 150 = 10P and **P = £15**. Substituting back: Qd = 120 − 60 = 60 and Qs = 90 − 30 = 60, so **Q = 60,000** per week. Always check that both equations give the same quantity.

At a price of £12: Qd = 120 − 48 = 72 and Qs = 72 − 30 = 42, so there is **excess demand of 30,000** units. At £18: Qd = 48 and Qs = 78, so **excess supply of 30,000** units.

If demand increases by 20,000 at every price, the new demand equation is Qd = 140 − 4P. Then 140 − 4P = 6P − 30, giving P = £17 and Q = 72,000. Price rises by about 13% and quantity by 20%. Showing the percentage changes lets you comment on elasticity, which is a quick route into evaluation.

sections.heading: Limitations of the model
sections.body:
The supply and demand model is powerful precisely because it is simple, but A* answers show awareness of what it leaves out.

- **Ceteris paribus is unrealistic.** In practice many determinants change at once, so observed price changes reflect several shifts that are hard to disentangle.
- **Markets may not be competitive.** The model assumes many buyers and sellers who are price takers. Where firms have market power (Theme 3), price is set by firms, not by the impersonal interaction of curves.
- **Prices may be sticky.** Menu costs, long-term contracts, regulation and concerns about fairness (for example, firms reluctant to raise prices in a crisis) slow adjustment.
- **Expectations and speculation** can make demand curves shift because of price changes themselves, as in housing or asset bubbles, so the market can move away from equilibrium for a period.
- **Information is imperfect.** Buyers and sellers do not know where equilibrium is; they discover it through trial and error, which takes time.

None of these destroys the model; they tell you when its predictions are most and least reliable, which is exactly what an evaluation paragraph should do.

key_terms.definition: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so the market clears and there is no pressure for price to change.
The quantity bought and sold at the equilibrium price.
A situation where, at the current price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (a shortage); it puts upward pressure on price.
A situation where, at the current price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded (a surplus); it puts downward pressure on price.
The pressures from buyers and sellers responding to shortages and surpluses that push price towards equilibrium.
A movement along a demand or supply curve caused by a change in the good's own price.
A movement of the whole demand or supply curve caused by a change in a non-price determinant, such as income or costs of production.
Any situation in which quantity demanded and quantity supplied are not equal at the prevailing price.
The assumption that all other influences are held constant while the effect of one variable is analysed.
A result that cannot be predicted from the direction of shifts alone, such as the price change when demand and supply both increase.

diagrams.title: Excess supply and excess demand
diagrams.caption: At P1 (above equilibrium) quantity demanded is Q1 and quantity supplied is Q2, so there is excess supply of Q2 − Q1 and price is pushed down. At P2 quantity demanded is Q2 but only Q1 is supplied, so excess demand pushes price up. Both pressures stop at E, where Pe and Qe clear the market.

diagrams.title: Increase in demand
diagrams.caption: A rise in demand shifts D1 to D2. At the old price P1 there is excess demand, so price is bid up and supply extends along S. Equilibrium moves from E1 to E2: price rises from P1 to P2 and quantity from Q1 to Q2.

diagrams.title: Decrease in supply
diagrams.caption: Higher costs shift supply left from S1 to S2. At P1 there is now excess demand, so price rises and demand contracts along D. Equilibrium moves from E1 to E2: price rises from P1 to P2 while quantity falls from Q1 to Q2.

diagrams.title: Simultaneous increase in demand and supply
diagrams.caption: Demand shifts from D1 to D2 and supply from S1 to S2 by the same amount. Quantity rises unambiguously from Q1 to Q2, but price is unchanged at P1. A larger demand shift would raise price; a larger supply shift would lower it, so the price effect is indeterminate.

formulae.name: Equilibrium condition
formulae.formula: Qd = Qs
formulae.example: Qd = 120 − 4P and Qs = 6P − 30: 120 − 4P = 6P − 30, so P = £15 and Q = 60 (thousand).

formulae.name: Excess demand
formulae.formula: Excess demand = Qd − Qs at a price below equilibrium
formulae.example: At P = £12: Qd = 72, Qs = 42, so excess demand = 30 (thousand units).

formulae.name: Excess supply
formulae.formula: Excess supply = Qs − Qd at a price above equilibrium
formulae.example: At P = £18: Qs = 78, Qd = 48, so excess supply = 30 (thousand units).

applications: UK housing: population growth, more single-person households and, until 2022, very low mortgage rates increased demand for homes, while planning constraints kept supply highly price inelastic. The result was rising prices and rents with only modest increases in housebuilding. When Bank Rate rose from 0.1% in late 2021 to 5.25% in 2023, mortgage costs jumped, demand fell and house prices dipped in 2023, showing demand-side shifts working in reverse.

Cocoa: poor harvests in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire (which together grow well over half the world's cocoa), linked to adverse weather and crop disease, cut supply sharply. With demand for chocolate very price inelastic in the short run, world cocoa prices rose above $10,000 a tonne in 2024, several times their level of a few years earlier. Chocolate makers responded with higher prices and smaller bars, passing part of the supply shock on to consumers.

Wholesale gas, 2021–22: recovering post-pandemic demand followed by the cut in Russian pipeline supply to Europe shifted demand right and supply left at the same time. Price rose dramatically (the determinate outcome), while the quantity effect was limited because demand for heating is price inelastic in the short run. The UK's Ofgem price cap meant the rise reached households with a lag.

Concert tickets: when Oasis announced reunion dates in 2024, demand at the face-value price vastly exceeded the fixed number of seats. The excess demand showed up as online queues, sell-outs within hours and resale prices far above face value. Ticketmaster's use of dynamic pricing (raising prices while fans were queuing) attracted a CMA investigation, a reminder that markets do not always reach equilibrium in a way consumers see as fair.

Globally, the price of lithium fell sharply in 2023 after new mines in Australia, South America and Africa and new refining capacity in China shifted supply right faster than demand for electric-vehicle batteries grew, illustrating the 'supply increase: price falls, quantity rises' case.
evaluation: Magnitude depends on elasticities: the same rightward shift in demand mostly raises price when supply is inelastic (housing, concert seats) but mostly raises quantity when supply is elastic (manufactured goods with spare capacity). Always say which case applies and why.

Time period: short-run supply is usually inelastic, so prices overshoot; in the long run, entry and investment shift supply and part of the price rise is reversed. A judgement should distinguish the immediate and long-term effects.
Simultaneous shifts make one outcome indeterminate. Strong answers state which variable is predictable and identify the information needed (relative size of the shifts) to predict the other.

Speed of adjustment varies: financial and commodity markets clear quickly, while labour, housing and ticketed events can stay in disequilibrium for long periods because of sticky prices, contracts or regulation.

Market structure matters: in concentrated markets (energy retail, supermarkets) firms set prices, so price may not respond in the way the competitive model predicts, for example 'rockets and feathers' pricing in fuel markets where prices rise quickly but fall slowly.

Ceteris paribus rarely holds, so real data show the net effect of several shifts. Attributing a price change to one cause is a claim that needs evidence, such as movements in quantity as well as price.
misconceptions: Writing 'price rises so demand falls' after a supply shock. The demand curve has not shifted; quantity demanded has contracted along an unchanged curve.
Shifting the demand curve in response to a change in the good's own price. Only non-price determinants shift a curve; own-price changes cause movements along it.
Thinking an increase in supply shifts the curve 'up'. An increase in supply shifts it to the right (down and to the right); a decrease shifts it left (up and to the left).
Assuming equilibrium is desirable. Equilibrium only means plans match; it can be inefficient (externalities) or inequitable (high rents).
Drawing both curve shifts in a simultaneous-change question and then claiming a definite change in both price and quantity. One of them is always indeterminate without more information.
exam_tips: Diagrams must be fully labelled: axes (Price, Quantity), D1/D2 or S1/S2, original and new equilibria, P1/P2 and Q1/Q2 on the axes with dashed lines, and an arrow showing the shift. An unlabelled diagram earns little.
In 5-mark 'explain' questions, write the adjustment chain: event → curve shifts (which way, why) → disequilibrium at old price → price change → extension/contraction → new equilibrium.
In data questions, use the figures: calculate percentage changes in price and quantity and comment on what they reveal about elasticity or which curve shifted.
For evaluation, the elasticity of the 'other' curve and the time period are almost always relevant and quick to explain with your diagram.
In multiple-choice questions on simultaneous shifts, eliminate options that claim a definite change in the indeterminate variable.

model_answer.question: With the help of a supply and demand diagram, examine the likely effects on the world cocoa market of a series of poor harvests in West Africa. (10 marks)
model_answer.answer:
The world cocoa market brings together cocoa farmers, mainly in West Africa, and buyers such as chocolate manufacturers. Equilibrium price is where the quantity of cocoa demanded equals the quantity supplied. Poor harvests caused by adverse weather and crop disease are a supply-side shock: at every price, farmers can deliver less cocoa, so the supply curve shifts left from S1 to S2.

On my diagram the original equilibrium is E1 at price P1 and quantity Q1. After the shift, at the old price P1 the quantity supplied falls to well below the quantity demanded, creating excess demand. Buyers compete for the limited beans, bidding up the price. As the price rises, quantity demanded contracts along the demand curve, as some manufacturers use less cocoa per bar or switch to cheaper recipes, until a new equilibrium E2 is reached at a higher price P2 and a lower quantity Q2.

The size of the price rise depends on price elasticity of demand. Cocoa makes up only a small share of the price of a chocolate bar and there are few substitutes for real cocoa, so demand is price inelastic in the short run. With a steep demand curve, most of the adjustment comes through price rather than quantity. This is consistent with what happened in 2024, when cocoa prices rose above $10,000 a tonne, several times their earlier level, while the quantity traded fell by a much smaller proportion.

The effects spread to related markets. Chocolate makers face higher costs, so supply of chocolate shifts left, raising chocolate prices; many firms also reduced bar sizes. Cocoa farmers with a reasonable crop may gain because the price rise outweighs the fall in quantity, since with inelastic demand total revenue to the industry rises, but farmers whose crops failed lose income. Many West African farmers also sell through state marketing boards at prices fixed in advance, so they may not receive much of the world price increase at all.

However, the effects depend on the time period. In the long run demand becomes more elastic as manufacturers reformulate products and consumers switch to other snacks, and high prices give an incentive to plant new trees or expand production in Latin America. Cocoa trees take several years to mature, so supply responds slowly, but in the long run supply should increase and push price back towards its earlier level. The magnitude also depends on whether the poor harvests are temporary or reflect longer-term climate change; if the shift is permanent, prices may stay higher for many years.

Overall, the most likely short-run effect is a large rise in price with a smaller fall in quantity, because demand is inelastic and supply cannot quickly respond, while the long-run effect is more moderate as both curves become more elastic.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definition of equilibrium and correct identification of a supply-side shock. Application: specific to cocoa (West Africa, 2024 price levels, reformulation, marketing boards) rather than a generic market. Analysis: a full chain from shift to excess demand to price rise and contraction, linked to the diagram with labelled equilibria, then extended through elasticity and related markets. Evaluation: short run versus long run, elasticity determining the split between price and quantity, the temporary versus permanent nature of the shock and the distribution of gains among farmers, ending with a supported judgement.

check.q: At a price below equilibrium, which of the following occurs?
options: The demand curve shifts left until the market clears
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and price rises
The supply curve shifts right until the market clears
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and price falls
check.explanation: Below equilibrium there is excess demand; competition among buyers raises price, causing an extension of supply and a contraction of demand. Neither curve shifts.

check.q: Demand for a good increases at the same time as its supply decreases. Which outcome is certain?
options: Price falls
Price rises
Quantity rises
Quantity falls
check.explanation: Both shifts put upward pressure on price. Quantity is indeterminate because the demand shift raises it and the supply shift lowers it.

check.q: Qd = 200 − 5P and Qs = 3P − 40. What is the equilibrium quantity?
Using the equations Qd = 200 − 5P and Qs = 3P − 40, what is the excess supply at a price of 35?
check.explanation: At P = 35: Qs = 105 − 40 = 65 and Qd = 200 − 175 = 25, so excess supply = 65 − 25 = 40.

check.q: A rise in demand leads to a large rise in price but only a small rise in quantity. This is most likely because:
options: Supply is price inelastic
Supply is price elastic
The good is inferior
Demand is price elastic
check.explanation: When supply is inelastic, producers cannot quickly increase output, so most of the adjustment to higher demand comes through price.

title: Price mechanism
overview: The price mechanism is the way changes in prices, driven by demand and supply, coordinate millions of independent decisions about what to produce, how and for whom. You need to explain its three functions (rationing, incentive and signalling), show them on a diagram, and recognise how it works in local, national and global markets. It is the foundation for understanding why markets can be efficient and, later in Theme 1, why they sometimes fail.
objectives: Explain the rationing, incentive and signalling functions of the price mechanism with examples
Use a supply and demand diagram to show all three functions operating after a change in market conditions
Distinguish short-run rationing from the long-run reallocation of resources
Compare how the price mechanism works in local, national and global markets
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of the price mechanism, including equity and market failure

sections.heading: What the price mechanism does
sections.body:
Every economy faces the basic economic problem: unlimited wants and scarce resources, so it must decide **what** to produce, **how** to produce it and **for whom**. In a command economy, planners answer these questions. In a market economy, they are answered by the **price mechanism**: the system in which the interaction of demand and supply sets prices, and changes in those prices automatically reallocate resources.

Adam Smith's 'invisible hand' captures the idea. No one coordinates the supply of bread to a city, yet bakers, millers, farmers and hauliers each respond to prices and profits, and bread appears on shelves. Friedrich Hayek emphasised the information problem: knowledge about local conditions, costs and preferences is dispersed among millions of people, and prices compress that knowledge into a single number that everyone can act on without knowing why it changed.

Economists usually describe three functions, which operate together rather than in sequence:

- **Signalling:** prices convey information about changes in scarcity and preferences.
- **Incentive:** price changes alter the rewards to producers and consumers, motivating them to change their behaviour.
- **Rationing:** prices allocate scarce goods among competing buyers, so that those willing and able to pay the most obtain them.

sections.heading: The signalling function
sections.body:
A rising price signals that a good has become relatively scarcer, either because demand has increased or supply has fallen. A falling price signals that it has become relatively more plentiful. These signals tell producers where resources are wanted and tell consumers which goods have become more costly to provide.

Signals work across markets as well as within them. When demand for electric vehicles rose, the higher prices and profits in battery supply chains signalled to mining companies that more lithium was needed, and to universities and workers that battery-engineering skills were valuable. A rising wage in a particular occupation is a price signal in the labour market, telling workers which skills to acquire.

The quality of the signal depends on the market. A price can only signal accurately if it reflects all costs and benefits. If a factory does not pay for the pollution it causes, its product is underpriced and the price signal is distorted: this is the route into market failure (1.3).

sections.heading: The incentive function
sections.body:
Signals matter only because they change incentives. Assuming firms aim to maximise profit, a higher price raises the potential profit from supplying a good, so existing firms expand output (an **extension of supply** along the curve in the short run) and, if supernormal profits persist, new firms enter and existing firms invest (a **rightward shift of supply** in the long run). A lower price reduces profits, encouraging firms to cut output and move resources elsewhere.

Consumers face incentives too. A higher price encourages them to economise, switch to substitutes or invest in alternatives. When UK energy prices surged in 2022, many households turned thermostats down and demand for heat pumps, insulation and solar panels rose, which are long-run incentive effects that outlast the price spike itself.

The incentive function is the key to dynamic efficiency: firms that innovate to cut costs or create products consumers value are rewarded with profit, while inefficient firms lose market share.

sections.heading: The rationing function
sections.body:
When a good becomes scarcer, there is not enough to satisfy everyone who wants it at the old price. A rise in price **rations** the available quantity: quantity demanded contracts until it matches what is available, and the good goes to those willing and able to pay the higher price. Without a price rise, scarce goods must be allocated by other means: queues, first-come-first-served, ballots, waiting lists, favouritism or black markets.

Rationing by price has an efficiency advantage. People who value the good most highly (as measured by willingness to pay) obtain it, and no time is wasted queuing. But willingness to pay depends on **ability to pay**. A wealthy household's willingness to pay for a concert ticket or a city-centre flat is not the same as a greater need. This is why governments often override price rationing for essentials: the NHS rations healthcare by need and waiting lists, not price, and social housing is allocated by priority need.

Note the time dimension. In the short run, when supply is inelastic, rationing is the main function at work: price rises to choke off demand. In the long run, the incentive function takes over as supply responds, and the eventual price rise is smaller.

sections.heading: All three functions on one diagram
sections.body:
Use a single diagram to show all three functions after an increase in demand (see the diagram).

- Demand shifts from D1 to D2. At P1 there is excess demand. **Rationing:** price rises to P2, which contracts quantity demanded so the limited supply goes to buyers willing to pay the most.
- **Signalling:** the higher price P2 and the resulting profits tell producers that consumers want more of this good.
- **Incentive:** in the short run firms extend supply along S1 to Q2. In the long run, supernormal profit attracts new entrants and investment, shifting supply to S2. Price falls back to P3 and quantity rises further to Q3.

This sequence explains how resources are reallocated: labour, capital and land move into industries where consumers want more output and away from those where demand is falling. In the diagram the long-run price ends up back at its original level, which happens when firms can expand at constant cost; if costs rise as the industry grows, the long-run price settles somewhere between P1 and P2.

sections.heading: Local, national and global markets
sections.body:
The specification asks you to consider the price mechanism in markets of different geographical scope.

- **Local markets:** a town's market for rented flats, a local car wash or hairdresser. Supply and demand depend on local conditions, and prices can differ greatly between areas: rents in London are far above those in the North East because demand is concentrated where jobs are. Information may be good (people know local prices), but supply can be very inelastic (land is fixed in a location), so rationing dominates.
- **National markets:** UK mortgages, the National Lottery, train travel. Prices reflect national conditions and often national regulation; for example, mortgage rates respond to Bank Rate set by the Bank of England.
- **Global markets:** crude oil, wheat, copper, cocoa, foreign currencies. Prices are set by world demand and supply and transmitted rapidly across countries. A drought in Brazil raises the price of coffee in UK supermarkets; a cut in OPEC+ output raises UK petrol prices. A small country is a **price taker** in these markets: UK consumers cannot influence the world price of oil.

The wider the market, the more numerous the buyers and sellers and, usually, the more effectively the price mechanism signals scarcity. But global markets also transmit shocks: a war or pandemic in one region can raise prices worldwide, as the 2022 surge in wheat and fertiliser prices after Russia's invasion of Ukraine showed.

sections.heading: Strengths and limitations
sections.body:
**Strengths:** the price mechanism is decentralised, needs no costly planning bureaucracy, responds quickly to change, provides incentives for efficiency and innovation, and respects consumer sovereignty, since resources follow what consumers choose to buy.

**Limitations:**

- **Market failure:** prices ignore external costs and benefits (1.3.2), cannot provide pure public goods (1.3.3) and may give misleading signals when information is incomplete (1.3.4).
- **Equity:** price rationing allocates by ability to pay. If the distribution of income is very unequal, the outcome may be efficient yet socially unacceptable, especially for necessities.
- **Market power:** monopolies and cartels can restrict output and raise prices, so prices signal the firm's market power rather than true scarcity.
- **Slow or volatile adjustment:** when supply is inelastic, signals cause large price swings (commodities) and the incentive response may come too late, as with housing.
- **Behavioural factors:** consumers do not always respond to prices rationally (1.2.10), and firms may hold prices down because of fairness concerns, weakening the rationing function.

This balance is why the UK is a **mixed economy**: the price mechanism allocates most goods, while the state intervenes where market outcomes are inefficient or inequitable.

key_terms.definition: The system by which the interaction of demand and supply determines prices, and changes in prices allocate resources between competing uses.
The role of price changes in conveying information to producers and consumers about changes in scarcity and preferences.
The role of price changes in altering the rewards to economic agents, encouraging producers to supply more of goods whose price has risen and consumers to economise on them.
The role of price in allocating a scarce good among competing buyers, so that it goes to those willing and able to pay the market price.
Adam Smith's metaphor for the way self-interested decisions of buyers and sellers, coordinated by prices, can produce an efficient allocation without central direction.
The idea that consumers' spending decisions determine what is produced in a market economy.
Allocation of scarce goods by methods other than price, such as queues, waiting lists, ballots or need-based criteria.
A market in which buyers and sellers are drawn from a limited geographical area, so price reflects local demand and supply conditions.
A market in which buyers and sellers across the world trade, so price reflects world demand and supply and individual small countries are price takers.
The way scarce factors of production are distributed among the production of different goods and services.

diagrams.title: Rationing, signalling and incentive functions
diagrams.caption: Demand rises from D1 to D2. In the short run price rises to P2, rationing the limited supply and signalling profit opportunities; supply extends to Q2. In the long run the incentive of supernormal profit brings entry, supply shifts to S2, and price falls to P3 while quantity rises to Q3.

diagrams.title: Rationing a fall in supply
diagrams.caption: A supply shock shifts S1 to S2. At the old price P1 the shortage would be Q1 − Qa. The price rise to P2 rations the good: quantity demanded contracts to Q2, so only buyers willing to pay P2 obtain it. The higher price also signals scarcity and gives other suppliers an incentive to enter.

applications: UK energy, 2022: the surge in wholesale gas prices signalled scarcity. Households and businesses had a strong incentive to cut use and invest in insulation and renewables, and UK gas demand fell noticeably in 2022–23. However, the government's Energy Price Guarantee capped the unit price paid by households (equivalent to about £2,500 a year for a typical household from October 2022), deliberately weakening the rationing function to protect living standards, at a large fiscal cost.

Local housing markets: rents differ hugely between UK regions because demand is concentrated where jobs are. High rents in London signal scarcity and ration housing to those able to pay, but the incentive function is weak because planning restrictions limit new building, so high prices persist rather than being competed away.

Global oil market: decisions by OPEC+ to cut production raise world oil prices, which are transmitted within days to UK forecourts. The UK is a price taker, so higher prices ration fuel among UK drivers and give an incentive to switch to electric vehicles and public transport over time.

Labour market: shortages of HGV drivers in the UK in 2021 pushed up drivers' pay substantially. The higher wage signalled scarcity and created an incentive for people to train as drivers, and the shortage eased over the following year, a clear example of the incentive function working with a lag.

Event tickets: many artists sell tickets below the market-clearing price for reputational and fairness reasons, so tickets are rationed by online queues and ballots instead. Resale at much higher prices shows the rationing function reasserting itself in the secondary market.
evaluation: Efficiency versus equity: price rationing allocates goods to those with the highest willingness to pay, which is efficient given the income distribution, but may be unacceptable for essentials like energy, housing and healthcare when incomes are very unequal.

Time lags: the incentive function often works slowly (housing, cocoa trees, training workers), so in the short run rationing dominates and prices can be very volatile. Whether the price mechanism 'works' depends on the time horizon considered.

Accuracy of signals: prices only signal true scarcity when markets are competitive, informed and free of externalities. With pollution, monopoly or information gaps, the mechanism allocates resources efficiently in a private sense but not a social sense.

Scope of the market: global markets with many traders give clearer signals but transmit external shocks quickly; local markets reflect local conditions but may be thin, with few sellers and inelastic supply.

Behavioural responses: consumers may not respond as predicted (habit, inertia, fairness concerns), and firms may avoid raising prices during crises to protect their reputation, weakening rationing and producing shortages.

Government intervention that suppresses price signals (price caps, rent controls) can protect consumers in the short run but may blunt incentives to economise and invest, so the long-run effects can be worse than the short-run benefit.
misconceptions: Treating the three functions as separate events in a fixed order. They operate simultaneously; a single price rise rations, signals and creates incentives at the same time.
Saying the incentive function means consumers have an incentive to buy more when price rises. A higher price gives producers an incentive to supply more and consumers an incentive to buy less.
Claiming the price mechanism always produces the best outcome. It allocates efficiently only under certain conditions and ignores equity.
Confusing willingness to pay with need. Price rationing allocates according to willingness and ability to pay, which depends on income.
Drawing a long-run supply shift in the opposite direction. Higher profit attracts entry, which shifts supply to the right, not the left.
exam_tips: Name the function you are using explicitly ('this illustrates the rationing function because...') and link it to the specific market in the question.
The demand-increase diagram with a long-run supply shift is the most efficient way to show all three functions; label short-run and long-run equilibria clearly.
When a question mentions a geographical scope (local, national, global), comment on how that scope affects the strength of signals, the number of buyers and sellers, and the elasticity of supply.
For evaluation, contrast efficiency with equity and short run with long run; these two angles are almost always relevant.
Price mechanism questions are often synoptic with market failure and government intervention: show you know where the mechanism breaks down.

model_answer.question: Assess the view that the price mechanism is the best way to allocate scarce resources such as tickets for major concerts. (12 marks)
model_answer.answer:
The price mechanism allocates resources through the interaction of demand and supply, with prices performing rationing, signalling and incentive functions. Concert tickets are a clear case of scarcity: the number of seats in a stadium is fixed, so supply is perfectly price inelastic for a given tour, while demand for a popular act can be enormous.

If tickets were sold at the market-clearing price, the price mechanism would ration the seats efficiently. On a diagram with a vertical supply curve at the stadium capacity, a high level of demand gives a high equilibrium price. Any lower price creates excess demand. Allowing price to rise to equilibrium contracts quantity demanded until it equals the number of seats, so tickets go to the fans with the highest willingness to pay. This avoids the costs of non-price rationing: the hours spent in online queues, the frustration of fans who miss out, and the profits captured by touts who buy at face value and resell at the market price. In that sense, when artists set prices below equilibrium, the price mechanism still operates, but in the secondary market, and the extra revenue goes to resellers rather than the artist or venue.

The signalling and incentive functions also matter. High prices signal strong demand, giving an incentive to add more dates or larger venues, effectively shifting supply to the right over time. When Oasis announced their 2024 reunion, very high demand led to additional dates being added, which is the incentive function at work.

However, there are strong arguments that price is not the best allocation method here. First, willingness to pay reflects ability to pay. A loyal fan on a low income may value the experience more, in terms of utility, than a wealthy casual buyer, but be outbid. Allocation by price is efficient given the existing income distribution, but not necessarily equitable. Second, consumers have strong views on fairness. The backlash against Ticketmaster's dynamic pricing in 2024, when prices rose while fans were queuing, and the subsequent CMA investigation, suggest that many fans see sudden price rises as exploitative. Behavioural economics shows that perceived unfairness can damage an artist's long-term reputation and future demand, so artists may rationally choose to sell below the market price. Third, the market is not competitive: a dominant ticketing platform may capture much of the surplus, so prices signal market power rather than pure scarcity.

Alternative methods include ballots, verified fan schemes and capping resale at face value. These spread access more evenly but create excess demand that must be managed and may encourage illegal resale if enforcement is weak.

On balance, the price mechanism is the most efficient way to allocate concert tickets in the narrow sense of matching tickets to willingness to pay and reducing waste from queuing and touting. But 'best' also involves fairness and the long-run relationship between artist and fans. Since concert tickets are a luxury rather than a necessity, equity concerns are weaker than for housing or energy, so a strong case exists for allowing prices to rise towards equilibrium, provided it is transparent, announced in advance rather than during the queue, and combined with limits on resale to stop touts capturing the surplus. The judgement depends on whether the artist values revenue or fan goodwill more.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: accurate definitions of the price mechanism and its functions. Application: specific features of concert tickets (fixed capacity, secondary market, dynamic pricing, CMA investigation, added dates). Analysis: the vertical supply diagram and the chain from below-equilibrium pricing to excess demand to touting; the incentive function shown by extra dates. Evaluation: equity versus efficiency, fairness and reputation (behavioural), market power, alternatives, and a conditional final judgement that depends on what is being maximised, which is what Level 3 evaluation requires.

check.q: A rise in the price of lithium encourages mining firms to open new mines. Which function of the price mechanism does this illustrate most directly?
options: Incentive
Stabilisation
Redistribution
Rationing
check.explanation: Higher prices increase potential profit, giving firms an incentive to expand capacity and enter the market.

check.q: Following a poor harvest, the price of strawberries rises and fewer consumers buy them. This is best described as:
options: The signalling function, because demand shifts left
The rationing function, because higher price contracts quantity demanded to match the reduced supply
The incentive function, because supply shifts right
Market failure, because some consumers cannot buy strawberries
check.explanation: The price rise allocates the smaller supply to those willing and able to pay; demand contracts along the curve rather than shifting.

check.q: Which of the following is a limitation of the price mechanism as a way of allocating resources?
options: It responds slowly because prices are set by the government
It provides no incentive for firms to cut costs
It requires a large planning bureaucracy
It allocates goods according to ability to pay rather than need
check.explanation: Price rationing gives goods to those willing and able to pay, which depends on income; this can be inequitable.

check.q: A small open economy such as the UK is best described as a price taker in which market?
options: The local market for haircuts in Leeds
The UK market for National Lottery tickets
The global market for crude oil
The market for council housing
check.explanation: The world oil price is set by global demand and supply; the UK's share is too small to influence it.

check.q: In the long run, an increase in demand for a product in a competitive market is most likely to lead to:
options: Permanent shortage
Fall in demand back to its original level
Leftward shift in supply as firms exit
Rightward shift in supply as new firms enter in response to profits
check.explanation: Supernormal profits attract entry, shifting supply right and moderating the initial price rise.

title: Consumer and producer surplus
overview: Consumer and producer surplus measure the net benefit that buyers and sellers gain from trading in a market. They turn the supply and demand diagram into a tool for judging welfare: who gains and who loses when prices change, and how much total welfare is lost when markets fail or governments intervene. Almost every later diagram in Theme 1 (taxes, subsidies, externalities, price controls) is evaluated with these areas.
objectives: Define consumer surplus and producer surplus and explain their link to marginal utility and marginal cost
Identify and shade consumer and producer surplus on a supply and demand diagram
Calculate consumer and producer surplus from a linear diagram
Analyse how shifts in demand and supply change consumer and producer surplus
Use surplus areas to discuss welfare, efficiency and distribution between stakeholders

sections.heading: Consumer surplus
sections.body:
**Consumer surplus** is the difference between the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay for a good and the price they actually pay. It is a measure of the extra utility (welfare) consumers gain from buying at the market price.

The demand curve shows willingness to pay for each successive unit. Because of **diminishing marginal utility** (1.2.2), the first units are valued very highly and later units less, so the demand curve slopes downward. If the market price is £5 and someone would have paid £9 for the first unit, they enjoy £4 of surplus on that unit. Adding up the surplus on every unit bought gives the area **below the demand curve and above the price line**, out to the quantity bought.

Consumer surplus explains everyday behaviour: why people feel they got a bargain, and why firms try to capture it by price discrimination (charging different prices to different customers, Theme 3) or through tiered pricing, such as peak and off-peak rail fares, that charge high-value customers more.

sections.heading: Producer surplus
sections.body:
**Producer surplus** is the difference between the price a producer receives and the minimum price at which they would have been willing to supply that unit. The supply curve shows that minimum price: in a competitive market it reflects the **marginal cost** of producing each extra unit.

If a firm would have supplied a unit for £2 (its marginal cost) and sells it for £5, it gains £3 of producer surplus on that unit. Summing over all units sold gives the area **above the supply curve and below the price line**, out to the quantity sold.

Producer surplus is not the same as profit. It is revenue minus the sum of marginal costs, so it excludes fixed costs. It is best thought of as the return to producers over and above what was needed to persuade them to supply each unit.

Together, consumer surplus plus producer surplus equals **total (community) surplus** or total welfare. In a competitive market with no externalities, total surplus is maximised at the equilibrium. Producing one unit fewer would sacrifice a unit valued above its cost; producing one more would cost more than consumers value it. This is the welfare basis for describing competitive equilibrium as **allocatively efficient**.

sections.heading: Reading and calculating the areas
sections.body:
With straight-line curves the areas are triangles (area = ½ × base × height).

Take the first diagram. Demand meets the price axis at £10, supply meets it at £2, and equilibrium is at a price of £5 and quantity of 5,000 units.

- Consumer surplus = ½ × 5,000 × (£10 − £5) = **£12,500**
- Producer surplus = ½ × 5,000 × (£5 − £2) = **£7,500**
- Total surplus = **£20,000**

When a price change creates a trapezium-shaped change, either split it into a rectangle and a triangle or use ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × width. Label areas with letters in your exam diagrams (for example 'area A + B') and refer to them in your writing; this is the clearest way to show which group gains or loses.

sections.heading: How changes in supply affect surplus
sections.body:
Suppose new technology lowers costs and supply increases from S1 to S2 (second diagram). Price falls from £5 to £4 and quantity rises from 5,000 to 6,000.

- **Consumers gain** in two ways: they pay £1 less on the 5,000 units they were already buying (a rectangle worth £5,000), and they gain surplus on the extra 1,000 units (a triangle worth ½ × 1,000 × £1 = £500). New consumer surplus = ½ × 6,000 × (£10 − £4) = £18,000, a gain of £5,500.
- **Producers** lose the £5,000 rectangle to consumers through the lower price but gain because their costs fell and they sell more. New producer surplus = ½ × 6,000 × (£4 − £0.40) = £10,800, which is higher than before.

So an increase in supply always raises consumer surplus, but its effect on producer surplus is **ambiguous**: it depends on how far costs fall relative to price, and on elasticity of demand. If demand is very inelastic, a supply increase causes a large price fall and producers can end up worse off. This is the farmer's paradox: a bumper harvest can reduce farm incomes.

sections.heading: How changes in demand affect surplus
sections.body:
An increase in demand (third diagram) raises price from £5 to £5.60 and quantity from 5,000 to 6,000. **Producer surplus rises unambiguously**: producers receive a higher price on the units they were already selling (the shaded strip) and gain surplus on extra units. New producer surplus = ½ × 6,000 × (£5.60 − £2) = £10,800, a rise of £3,300.

The effect on consumer surplus is more subtle. Existing buyers pay more, which reduces their surplus, but the shift itself reflects a rise in willingness to pay (for example because of higher incomes), so measured consumer surplus under the new demand curve can rise. Here new consumer surplus is ½ × 6,000 × (£11.60 − £5.60) = £18,000. Be careful in the exam to separate the loss suffered by buyers who were already in the market from the change in the total area.

Conversely, a fall in demand reduces producer surplus, and a fall in supply (higher costs, a poor harvest) raises price and unambiguously reduces consumer surplus.

sections.heading: Why surplus matters: welfare and distribution
sections.body:
Surplus analysis is the toolkit for judging interventions and market failures:

- **Deadweight (welfare) loss** is surplus lost to society because output differs from the efficient level. Taxes, price controls and externalities all create triangles of lost surplus (1.2.9, 1.3.2, 1.4.1).
- **Transfers** are areas that move from one group to another (for example from consumers to the government as tax revenue) without being lost to society as a whole.
- **Distribution** matters as well as size. A policy that increases total surplus but transfers large amounts from low-income consumers to shareholders may be judged undesirable on equity grounds.

Two important caveats. First, £1 of surplus to a poor household and £1 to a rich one are treated as equal, although diminishing marginal utility of income suggests the poor household gains more utility. Second, the demand curve measures private willingness to pay, so if consumers are poorly informed or behave irrationally (1.2.10, 1.3.4), measured consumer surplus may not reflect true welfare.

key_terms.definition: The difference between the maximum price consumers are willing to pay and the price they actually pay; the area below the demand curve and above the market price.
The difference between the price producers receive and the minimum price at which they would be willing to supply; the area above the supply curve and below the market price.
The sum of consumer surplus and producer surplus, used as a measure of the total net welfare generated by a market.
The maximum amount a consumer would pay for a unit of a good, shown by the height of the demand curve at that quantity.
The loss of total surplus that occurs when output is not at the allocatively efficient level, for example because of a tax, price control or externality.
A situation where resources are allocated so that total surplus is maximised, occurring where the value consumers place on the last unit equals its marginal cost.
The fall in additional satisfaction from consuming each extra unit of a good, which explains why the demand curve, and so consumer surplus, has its shape.

diagrams.title: Consumer and producer surplus
diagrams.caption: At equilibrium (P = 5, Q = 5) consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price; producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price. Together they form total surplus, which is maximised at the competitive equilibrium.

diagrams.title: Increase in supply: gain in consumer surplus
diagrams.caption: Supply rises from S1 to S2, so price falls from P1 to P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2. The shaded strip is the gain in consumer surplus: a rectangle on existing purchases plus a triangle on extra units. The effect on producer surplus depends on how far costs fall relative to price.

diagrams.title: Increase in demand: gain in producer surplus
diagrams.caption: Demand rises from D1 to D2, so price rises from P1 to P2 and quantity from Q1 to Q2. The shaded strip is the gain in producer surplus: a higher price on existing sales plus surplus on the extra units.

formulae.name: Consumer surplus (linear demand)
formulae.formula: CS = ½ × quantity × (price-axis intercept of demand − market price)
formulae.example: Demand meets the price axis at £10, P = £5, Q = 5,000: CS = ½ × 5,000 × £5 = £12,500.

formulae.name: Producer surplus (linear supply)
formulae.formula: PS = ½ × quantity × (market price − price-axis intercept of supply)
formulae.example: Supply meets the price axis at £2, P = £5, Q = 5,000: PS = ½ × 5,000 × £3 = £7,500.

formulae.name: Change in CS when price falls
formulae.formula: ΔCS = (fall in price × original quantity) + ½ × fall in price × increase in quantity

applications: Lithium: as new mines and refining capacity expanded supply in 2023, lithium prices fell by more than three quarters from their late-2022 peak. Battery and electric-vehicle makers gained consumer surplus (lower input costs), while many higher-cost producers saw producer surplus collapse, with some mines in Australia and elsewhere cutting output or pausing operations, an example of producer surplus falling when inelastic demand meets a large supply increase.

UK energy, 2022: the sharp rise in wholesale gas prices reduced household consumer surplus dramatically while raising the producer surplus of gas producers and some electricity generators. The Energy Profits Levy introduced in 2022 was a windfall tax designed to transfer part of this producer surplus back to the government to help fund household support.

Price discrimination: train operators and airlines use advance, off-peak and anytime fares to charge customers closer to their willingness to pay, converting consumer surplus into producer revenue. Business travellers with inelastic demand pay anytime fares; leisure travellers with elastic demand buy cheaper advance tickets.

Streaming services: as more providers entered the market, consumers gained surplus from choice and competition. Later price rises and the introduction of advertising tiers can be seen as firms attempting to capture back some of that surplus.

Globally, the shale revolution in the USA increased oil and gas supply in the 2010s, lowering energy prices for consumers worldwide and raising consumer surplus, while reducing producer surplus for higher-cost producers elsewhere.
evaluation: Elasticity determines the distribution of gains: with inelastic demand, a supply increase transfers a large amount of surplus from producers to consumers, possibly leaving producers worse off; with elastic demand, producers gain from higher volumes.

Surplus is a money measure and ignores distribution: £1 of surplus is counted the same whether it goes to a low-income household or a wealthy shareholder, so an efficient outcome may not be equitable.
Demand curves may not measure true benefit: with information gaps, habits or addiction, willingness to pay can overstate or understate welfare, so consumer surplus is an imperfect guide.
Externalities are excluded: private surplus ignores third-party costs and benefits, so maximising consumer plus producer surplus does not maximise social welfare when externalities are significant.

Precision is limited in practice: real demand and supply curves are not linear or observable, so estimates of surplus (used, for example, in transport cost-benefit analysis) are approximations based on assumptions.
Time period: producer surplus gains from a demand increase may be competed away in the long run as new firms enter, while consumers' gains from cost-reducing innovation tend to be permanent.
misconceptions: Shading consumer surplus below the price line. CS is above the price and below the demand curve; PS is below the price and above the supply curve.
Equating producer surplus with profit. Producer surplus excludes fixed costs, so it is larger than profit.
Assuming a fall in price must reduce producer surplus. If the fall is caused by lower costs (a supply shift), producer surplus can rise.
Treating tax revenue as a deadweight loss. Revenue is a transfer from consumers and producers to the government; only the triangle of lost trades is deadweight loss.
Forgetting to stop the surplus areas at the quantity actually traded. Surplus only exists on units that are bought and sold.
exam_tips: Label areas with letters on your diagram and write, for example, 'consumer surplus falls by area A + B'. This is precise and saves words.
In 4- or 5-mark calculation questions, show the formula, substitution and units (£). Many marks are lost by forgetting that quantities are in thousands.
Use surplus to quantify winners and losers in intervention questions; it turns a descriptive answer into an analytical one.
When evaluating, comment on the distribution of surplus (who gains, who loses) and on whether the demand curve reflects true welfare.
Link consumer surplus to diminishing marginal utility and producer surplus to marginal cost to show depth of understanding.

model_answer.question: With the help of a diagram, examine the likely effects on consumer and producer surplus of a large increase in the world supply of lithium caused by the opening of new mines. (8 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Consumer surplus is the difference between what buyers are willing to pay and what they actually pay, shown by the area below demand and above price. Producer surplus is the difference between the price received and the minimum price producers would accept, shown by the area above supply and below price.

New mines increase the world supply of lithium, shifting supply from S1 to S2. At the original price P1 there is excess supply, so price falls to P2 and quantity demanded by battery manufacturers extends from Q1 to Q2.

Consumers of lithium, mainly battery and electric-vehicle makers, unambiguously gain. Their surplus rises by the area between P1 and P2 bounded by the demand curve: a rectangle representing the lower price on the original quantity Q1, plus a triangle of surplus on the extra units Q1 to Q2. Lower input costs may be passed on through cheaper batteries, raising surplus in related markets such as electric vehicles.

The effect on producer surplus is ambiguous. Existing producers lose the rectangle between P1 and P2 on the original quantity, which is transferred to consumers. However, the new low-cost mines gain surplus because their marginal costs are below the new price. The net effect depends on price elasticity of demand. Demand for lithium is price inelastic in the short run because batteries cannot easily switch to alternative chemistries, so the supply increase causes a large fall in price relative to the rise in quantity. This happened in 2023, when lithium prices fell by more than three quarters from their peak, so producer surplus for many existing high-cost mines fell sharply and some suspended production.

Overall, consumers gain substantially, total surplus rises because more is traded at a lower cost, but producer surplus is likely to fall for established producers while rising for new low-cost entrants. In the long run, demand may become more elastic as cheaper batteries expand the electric-vehicle market, which would moderate the price fall and allow producers to recover some of their lost surplus.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definitions of both surpluses. Application: lithium buyers, battery makers, 2023 price collapse, high-cost mines suspending output. Analysis: correct supply shift, clear identification of rectangle and triangle areas, and the transfer from producers to consumers. Evaluation: ambiguity of the producer-surplus effect explained through elasticity, a distinction between existing and new producers, and a short-run versus long-run judgement. For an 8-mark examine question this is enough evaluation to reach the top level.

check.q: On a supply and demand diagram, consumer surplus is the area:
options: Below the supply curve
Below the demand curve and above the price
Between the demand and supply curves to the right of equilibrium
Above the supply curve and below the price
check.explanation: Consumer surplus is willingness to pay (demand) minus the price paid, summed over all units bought.

check.q: Demand meets the price axis at £20 and supply at £4. Equilibrium price is £12 and quantity is 400. What is producer surplus?
check.explanation: PS = ½ × 400 × (£12 − £4) = £1,600. Consumer surplus would be ½ × 400 × (£20 − £12) = £1,600 as well.

check.q: A rise in the costs of production shifts supply to the left. Which is certain?
options: Consumer surplus rises
Total surplus rises
Consumer surplus falls
Producer surplus rises
check.explanation: Price rises and quantity falls, so consumers pay more for fewer units; consumer surplus definitely falls. The effect on producer surplus is ambiguous.

check.q: Why is producer surplus not the same as profit?
options: Producer surplus is measured at the consumer price
Producer surplus ignores fixed costs
Producer surplus includes tax revenue
Profit ignores revenue
check.explanation: Producer surplus is revenue minus the sum of marginal (variable) costs, so it excludes fixed costs and exceeds profit.

check.q: An increase in demand raises price from £8 to £10 and quantity from 1,000 to 1,400. What is the increase in producer surplus?
check.explanation: Rectangle: £2 × 1,000 = £2,000 on existing units, plus triangle ½ × 400 × £2 = £400 on new units, a total of £2,400.

title: Indirect taxes and subsidies
overview: Indirect taxes and subsidies change producers' costs and so shift the supply curve. This topic asks you to show, on accurate diagrams, how a specific or ad valorem tax and a per-unit subsidy change price and quantity, who bears the tax (incidence), how much revenue the government raises or spends, and how the outcome depends on elasticity. It is one of the most heavily examined areas of Theme 1, with calculations in multiple-choice and short-answer questions and diagrams in almost every intervention essay.
objectives: Distinguish specific and ad valorem indirect taxes and draw the correct supply shift for each
Show and calculate the incidence of a tax on consumers and producers, total tax revenue and the deadweight loss
Explain how price elasticity of demand and supply determine tax incidence
Show and calculate the effect of a per-unit subsidy, including the total cost to government and the shares of consumers and producers
Analyse the impact of taxes and subsidies on consumers, producers, government and third parties, with UK examples
Evaluate the effectiveness of taxes and subsidies using elasticity, time period and stakeholder arguments

sections.heading: Indirect taxes: specific and ad valorem
sections.body:
An **indirect tax** is a tax on spending on goods and services. It is collected from firms by HMRC, but firms pass on part of it to consumers through higher prices. (A direct tax, such as income tax, is levied on income and paid directly by the person who earns it.)

- A **specific (unit) tax** is a fixed amount per unit sold, regardless of price: UK fuel duty of around 53p per litre (frozen at that rate since a 5p cut in 2022), duty on a packet of cigarettes, the Soft Drinks Industry Levy of 18p or 24p per litre depending on sugar content. It shifts the supply curve **vertically upwards by the amount of the tax**, so the new curve is **parallel** to the original.
- An **ad valorem tax** is a percentage of the price: VAT at the standard rate of 20%. Because the tax per unit is larger at higher prices, the supply curve **pivots**: the vertical gap between the original and new curves widens as price rises.

Why does the supply curve shift? From the firm's point of view, the tax is an extra cost of selling each unit. To be willing to supply any given quantity, the firm must now receive the original supply price plus the tax. So supply decreases (shifts left/upwards). Note that it is the **supply** curve that shifts, not demand: consumers' willingness to pay has not changed.

Many goods carry both. A litre of petrol bears fuel duty (specific) and then VAT at 20% on the duty-inclusive price (ad valorem), so around half of the pump price is tax.

sections.heading: The effect of a specific tax: incidence, revenue and welfare
sections.body:
Work through the first diagram, which uses illustrative numbers (P in £, Q in thousands per week). Before the tax, equilibrium is at £5 and 5,000 units. A specific tax of £2.50 per unit shifts supply up by £2.50 to S + tax.

- At the old price there is now excess demand, so price rises. The new equilibrium is where S + tax cuts demand: consumers pay **£6.50** and quantity falls to **3,750**.
- Producers receive the consumer price minus the tax: £6.50 − £2.50 = **£4.00**, which is the point on the original supply curve at 3,750 units.
- **Total tax revenue** = tax per unit × quantity = £2.50 × 3,750 = **£9,375** (the whole rectangle between £6.50 and £4.00).
- **Consumer incidence** = (£6.50 − £5.00) × 3,750 = **£5,625**, or 60% of the revenue.
- **Producer incidence** = (£5.00 − £4.00) × 3,750 = **£3,750**, or 40%.

The **incidence** of a tax describes who ultimately bears it, which is different from who legally pays it to HMRC (the formal incidence). Consumers bear the part reflected in a higher price; producers bear the part reflected in a lower net price received.

**Welfare.** Consumer surplus falls by the consumer-incidence rectangle plus a small triangle; producer surplus falls by the producer-incidence rectangle plus a small triangle. The rectangles are transferred to the government as revenue. The two triangles together are the **deadweight loss**: trades between 3,750 and 5,000 that would have benefited both sides no longer take place. Here it is ½ × £2.50 × 1,250 = **£1,562.50**. (If the good creates negative externalities, the reduction in output may actually be a welfare gain, which is the whole case for corrective taxes in 1.4.1.)

sections.heading: Elasticity and incidence
sections.body:
The share of the tax borne by each side depends on relative elasticities. The rule: **the more price inelastic side of the market bears the greater share of the tax.**

- If demand is **price inelastic** (few substitutes, habit-forming or necessary goods such as fuel, tobacco and alcohol), consumers continue buying even when price rises, so firms can pass most of the tax on. The first diagram shows this: consumers bear 60%.
- If demand is **price elastic** (many substitutes, such as one brand of crisps or a particular holiday destination), firms cannot raise price much without losing many sales, so they absorb most of the tax. In the fourth diagram a £2.40 tax raises the consumer price by only 80p (one third) while producers' net price falls by £1.60 (two thirds).
- If supply is inelastic (for example, fixed short-run capacity), producers bear more; if supply is elastic, more falls on consumers.

A useful approximation: consumers' share ≈ PES ÷ (PES + PED), using the absolute value of PED. In the first diagram, at the original equilibrium PED is about −0.83 and PES is 1.25, giving a consumer share of 1.25 ÷ 2.08 ≈ 0.6.

Elasticity also determines what the tax **achieves**. With inelastic demand, quantity falls little and revenue is high, so the tax is a good **revenue raiser** but a weak **behaviour changer**. With elastic demand, the reverse holds. This trade-off is central to evaluating tobacco, fuel, sugar and carbon taxes.

sections.heading: Ad valorem taxes
sections.body:
Because an ad valorem tax is a percentage of price, the supply curve pivots upwards and becomes steeper (second diagram). With a 25% tax in the illustration, the consumer price rises from £5.00 to about £5.68 and quantity falls from 5,000 to about 4,430; producers receive about £4.55, so the tax per unit at the new equilibrium is about £1.14 (25% of £4.55).

Two exam points follow:

- An ad valorem tax raises more per unit on expensive versions of a product, which can be seen as progressive within a product category (a luxury car pays more VAT than a cheap one). Conversely, a specific tax is a larger percentage of the price of cheap products, so it hits budget brands hardest. This is why cigarette duty combines a specific element with an ad valorem element and a minimum excise tax.
- Revenue from ad valorem taxes rises automatically with inflation, whereas specific duties must be uprated by the Chancellor. Repeated freezes of fuel duty since 2011 mean its real value has fallen considerably.

sections.heading: Subsidies: effects, incidence and cost
sections.body:
A **subsidy** is a payment by the government to producers (or sometimes consumers) to lower costs and encourage production or consumption. A per-unit subsidy shifts the supply curve **vertically downwards by the amount of the subsidy**.

In the third diagram a subsidy of £2 per unit shifts supply from S to S − subsidy. Using the same demand and supply as the first diagram:

- Price paid by consumers falls from £5.00 to **£3.80**; quantity rises from 5,000 to **6,000**.
- Producers receive the consumer price plus the subsidy: £3.80 + £2.00 = **£5.80**.
- **Total cost to the government** = £2 × 6,000 = **£12,000** (the whole shaded rectangle).
- Consumers' share = (£5.00 − £3.80) × 6,000 = **£7,200** (60%); producers' share = (£5.80 − £5.00) × 6,000 = **£4,800** (40%).

As with taxes, the more inelastic side of the market gains the larger share. If demand is inelastic, consumers gain most through lower prices but quantity rises little, so a subsidy aimed at increasing consumption is not very effective. If supply is inelastic, much of the subsidy raises producers' incomes without much extra output.

In the absence of any externality, a subsidy also creates a deadweight loss: units between 5,000 and 6,000 cost more to produce (shown by the original supply curve) than consumers value them (shown by demand). Here that loss is ½ × £2 × 1,000 = £1,000. Subsidies are therefore justified on efficiency grounds only when the good generates **positive externalities** or when there are equity goals, such as supporting low-income households.

sections.heading: Impact on stakeholders
sections.body:
Examiners reward answers that go beyond the diagram to consider each group:

- **Consumers:** higher prices and lower consumption with a tax; indirect taxes are often **regressive** because lower-income households spend a larger share of income on taxed goods such as tobacco and fuel. With a subsidy, consumers gain through lower prices.
- **Producers:** lower net price and sales, so lower revenue and profits; possible job losses; incentive to reformulate or innovate to avoid the tax (as with the sugar levy). Subsidies raise revenue and may reduce the incentive to become efficient.
- **Government:** tax revenue (fuel duty raises around £25 billion a year) that can fund public services or hypothecated spending; subsidies have an opportunity cost, since the money could be used for healthcare or education or require higher taxes or borrowing.
- **Third parties and the wider economy:** taxes on harmful goods can reduce external costs; taxes raise measured inflation (CPI); subsidies to green technology can reduce emissions and build new industries.

Remember that the government's revenue depends on how far quantity falls. A tax that works perfectly at changing behaviour raises little money: the sugar levy was expected to raise around £500 million a year but raised less because many manufacturers reformulated their drinks.

key_terms.definition: A tax on expenditure on goods and services, collected from producers, part of which is passed on to consumers through higher prices.
An indirect tax of a fixed amount per unit sold, which shifts the supply curve vertically upward by the amount of the tax, parallel to the original.
An indirect tax levied as a percentage of the price of a good, such as VAT, which pivots the supply curve so the gap widens at higher prices.
The distribution of the burden of a tax between consumers (through higher prices) and producers (through a lower net price received).
Who is legally responsible for paying a tax to the authorities, which may differ from who actually bears its burden.
A payment from the government to producers or consumers that lowers the cost of production or consumption, shifting the supply curve vertically down by the amount per unit.
Tax per unit multiplied by the quantity sold after the tax is imposed.
The loss of consumer and producer surplus from trades that no longer take place (or take place inefficiently) because of a tax or subsidy, not offset by any gain elsewhere.
A tax that takes a larger proportion of income from low-income households than from high-income households.
A tax whose revenue is earmarked for a specific purpose, such as using sugar levy revenue for school sport.

diagrams.title: Specific tax: incidence and revenue
diagrams.caption: A specific tax shifts S up by the tax to S+tax. Consumer price rises from P1 to P2 and quantity falls from Q1 to Q2; producers receive P3 (P2 minus the tax). The upper rectangle is the consumers' share of tax revenue, the lower one the producers' share, and the triangle is the deadweight loss. Demand is less elastic than supply here, so consumers bear the larger share.

diagrams.title: Ad valorem tax
diagrams.caption: An ad valorem tax is a percentage of price, so S pivots to S+tax and the vertical gap between the curves (the tax per unit) widens as price rises. Consumer price rises from P1 to P2, quantity falls to Q2, and producers receive P3.

diagrams.title: Per-unit subsidy
diagrams.caption: A subsidy shifts S down by the subsidy per unit. Consumer price falls from P1 to P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2; producers receive P3 (P2 plus the subsidy). The whole rectangle between P3 and P2 up to Q2 is the cost to government: the lower part is passed to consumers, the upper part kept by producers.

diagrams.title: Tax incidence with elastic demand
diagrams.caption: With price elastic demand, firms cannot pass much of the tax on without losing many sales. Consumer price rises only from P1 to P2, while the price producers receive falls from P1 to P3, so producers bear the larger share and quantity falls proportionally more.

formulae.name: Tax revenue
formulae.formula: Tax per unit × quantity sold after tax

formulae.name: Consumer incidence
formulae.formula: (New consumer price − original price) × new quantity

formulae.name: Producer incidence
formulae.formula: (Original price − price received by producers) × new quantity

formulae.name: Total cost of a subsidy
formulae.formula: Subsidy per unit × quantity sold after subsidy

formulae.name: Approximate consumer share of a tax
formulae.formula: PES ÷ (PES + |PED|)
formulae.example: PES = 1.25 and PED = −0.83: 1.25 ÷ 2.08 ≈ 0.6, so consumers bear about 60%.

applications: Soft Drinks Industry Levy (from April 2018): a specific tax of 18p per litre on drinks with 5g–8g of sugar per 100ml and 24p above 8g, paid by producers and importers. Because it was announced two years in advance, many firms reformulated to fall below the thresholds, so the sugar content of drinks covered by the levy fell by over 40%. This is an example of a tax changing producer behaviour rather than mainly consumer prices, and of revenue being lower than first forecast.

Fuel duty and VAT: petrol and diesel carry a specific duty of around 53p per litre plus 20% VAT. Demand is price inelastic in the short run, so most of the tax falls on motorists and revenue is large and reliable, but the effect on emissions is limited. Successive governments have frozen the duty since 2011, partly because of its regressive impact on rural and lower-income drivers.

Tobacco duty combines a specific element, an ad valorem element (a percentage of retail price) and a minimum excise tax. The mix targets cheaper brands, which a purely ad valorem tax would leave relatively lightly taxed. High duties also encourage smuggling and illicit sales, which HMRC estimates account for a significant share of tobacco consumed.

Subsidies: the Boiler Upgrade Scheme offers grants (raised to £7,500 in 2023) towards the cost of heat pumps, and the government reintroduced a grant for some new electric cars in 2025. The £2 (later £3) cap on single bus fares in England from 2023 was funded by payments to bus operators, effectively a per-journey subsidy that lowered prices to passengers.

Globally, the IMF estimates that explicit fossil-fuel subsidies (keeping fuel prices below cost) run to hundreds of billions of dollars a year, encouraging overconsumption of carbon-intensive energy. In contrast, the USA's Inflation Reduction Act used tax credits worth up to $7,500 per electric vehicle (until 2025) to stimulate demand for low-carbon goods.
evaluation: Elasticity is decisive: with inelastic demand a tax raises revenue but barely changes behaviour and falls mainly on consumers; with elastic demand it changes behaviour but raises less revenue and hurts producers. Identify which objective the government is pursuing before judging success.
